transcript: Interviewer: I'm Rachel, the Store Manager, and this interview should take about fifteen minutes, can you tell me a little about yourself?

Me: I've been in retail about five years. Right now I'm a shift lead at Corner Market, a small neighborhood grocery, where I run the register, train new cashiers and handle the morning deliveries. Before that I worked two years in a warehouse picking orders. I'm looking for a bigger store with more hours.
Interviewer: You've got some good experience, now can you tell me about a time when you had to answer a lot of customer questions about products?
Me: I'm pretty good with customers I guess.
Interviewer: Can you give me an example of a time when you had to help a customer find something or answer a question about a product?

Me: A guy came in really upset because we'd charged him twice for a case of water. I said sorry right away, checked the receipt, and saw the double scan. I refunded him on the spot and gave him a coupon. He calmed down and he still comes in every week.
Interviewer: How did you handle the cash register part of that, to make sure the refund was done correctly?
Me: I count three drawers every night and they've balanced every time. I count twice and keep big bills under the tray.
Interviewer: That's good to hear about your cash handling, now can you tell me about a time when you received a large delivery and had to stock shelves quickly to get ready for customers?

Me: One night my drawer was twenty dollars short when I counted it. I recounted, then went back through the receipts and found a refund I'd keyed wrong. I fixed it in the system and wrote it up for my manager so it wouldn't happen again.
Interviewer: That's a great example of catching a mistake, but I was asking about receiving a delivery, can you tell me about a time when you had to stock shelves after a delivery?
Me: When we got two new cashiers the same week before Thanksgiving, I made a one page cheat sheet for the register and stood next to each of them for their first few shifts.

Interviewer: That's helpful training, now what would you do if you were restocking shelves and a customer asked you where something was, but you were in the middle of putting away a big pallet of merchandise?
Me: I'd stay calm, listen to the whole problem first, and fix what I can right there. If it's something I can't fix, like a big refund, I'd get the manager and stay with the customer.
Interviewer: The job posting mentions being able to lift 40 pounds, can you tell me about a time when you had to lift something heavy at work, and how you did it safely?
Me: Yes. I lift cases all day now, and in the warehouse I loaded trucks every shift.
Interviewer: Do you have any questions for me about the Store Associate position or Maple Grocers?
Me: What does a good first month look like for someone in this job? And how are shifts scheduled?

Interviewer: A good first month would be getting familiar with our store and products, and providing great customer service. Shifts are scheduled a week in advance, and we try to give everyone a mix of days and hours. Thank you for coming in today

data.summary: You have relevant experience and skills for the Store Associate position, but struggled to provide specific examples for some of the interviewer's questions, which may raise concerns about your ability to think on your feet. You were able to showcase your customer service skills and experience with cash handling, but could improve on providing more detailed and relevant examples for certain scenarios
good: You provided a good example of handling a customer complaint and resolving the issue efficiently
You demonstrated experience with cash handling and inventory management
fix: For the question about answering customer questions, try to provide a more specific example of a time when you had to answer multiple questions about products, such as describing a situation where you helped a customer find a specific item or explained the features of a product

When asked about receiving a large delivery and stocking shelves, focus on providing a relevant example from your experience, such as describing a time when you had to quickly stock shelves after a delivery to prepare for customers

interviews.job: Front Desk Receptionist at Bright Smile Dental
transcript: Interviewer: I'm Karen, the Office Manager here at Bright Smile Dental. This interview should take about fifteen minutes, and I'd like to start by asking you to tell me a little bit about yourself.

Me: I've worked with people for about four years. I was a server at Casa Verde for three years and then I worked at DesertLink's call center, answering billing and outage calls. I took medical office classes at Pima this year because I want to work in healthcare.

Interviewer: You've had experience dealing with customers and you're looking to transition into healthcare, that's great. Can you tell me about your experience with scheduling, since that's a big part of this front desk role?
Me: I'm organized, I think.
Interviewer: Being organized is important, but can you give me an example of a time when you actually scheduled appointments or managed a schedule in one of your previous jobs?

Me: At the call center a customer called furious because his internet had been out for three days and he works from home. I apologized, checked the outage map, and saw his area was fixed but his modem wasn't. I walked him through a reset and when that didn't work I booked a tech for the next morning. He thanked me at the end of the call.

Interviewer: That sounds like a tough call to handle, but you seemed to resolve the issue for him. Tell me about a time when you had to handle a sensitive or confidential situation, since we deal with patient records and insurance information here.

Me: At Casa Verde we got slammed one Friday when two servers called out. I took two extra tables and asked the host to seat my section in waves so the kitchen wouldn't get buried. We got through the night without anyone walking out.
Interviewer: It sounds like you helped manage a chaotic situation. What would you do if a patient was upset because their insurance wasn't covering a procedure and they couldn't pay out of pocket?
Me: I'd smile, tell the patient in the lobby I'll be right with them, put the caller on a short hold, and check the patient in. Then I'd go back to the phone.

Interviewer: That's a good start, but how would you actually address the patient's concern about their insurance and payment? 

Also, I noticed your resume doesn't mention experience with Dentrix or similar scheduling software, can you tell me about any experience you have with software like that?
Me: When Salesforce changed at work, I made notes for myself and shared them with two new people.
Interviewer: That's helpful, but I'm not seeing any direct experience with Dentrix. Do you have any questions for me about the position or Bright Smile Dental?
Me: What software do you use for scheduling, and is there training for it?
Interviewer: We use Dentrix, and yes, we provide training for all new staff members to get them up to speed on our systems. Thank you for coming in today, I appreciate your time

data.summary: You presented yourself as a customer-focused and organized individual with a desire to transition into healthcare, but struggled to provide specific examples of scheduling and handling sensitive situations, which are crucial for the Front Desk Receptionist role at Bright Smile Dental. A hiring manager would see you as a potential candidate with some relevant experience, but in need of further training and development to excel in the position
good: You effectively handled a tough call at the call center and resolved the issue for the customer
You asked relevant questions about the position, such as the software used for scheduling and the availability of training
fix: Provide more specific examples of scheduling appointments or managing a schedule in your previous jobs, as seen in your response to the question about scheduling experience
Develop a more comprehensive approach to handling sensitive or confidential situations, such as the scenario with the patient's insurance not covering a procedure
Be more prepared to discuss your experience with software similar to Dentrix, even if it's not directly related, to show your ability to learn and adapt to new systems
